why: The root. Indexing, iteration, and the hash map — the container every later topic reaches for when it needs O(1) lookup.
Once you can walk an array, walk it with two indices. The first technique that beats a nested loop without extra memory.
A second way to hold state while scanning: keep what you might still need, discard what you never will.
Precompute once, answer range queries in O(1). The idea that trading memory for time is a choice you get to make.
Digits, divisors, overflow, and modular arithmetic — needs no data structure, so it can be picked up early.
Independent of everything else: masks, shifts, and n & (n-1). Cheap to learn, and it turns up inside DP and Tries later.
Two converging pointers with a decision in the middle. Generalises from 'find a value' to 'find a boundary' to 'search an answer space'.
Two pointers moving the same direction, plus a running aggregate. Where the two ideas below it meet.
Pointers without random access. Slow/fast is two-pointers again, and relinking nodes is the first taste of mutating a structure.
Scanning with an index and a fallback. KMP's failure function is the payoff for understanding the naive scan first.
The hinge of the whole map. A linked structure (from Linked Lists) that branches, searched by halving (from Binary Search). Everything below depends on it.
Binary search wearing a tree costume — the ordering invariant is what makes it O(height) instead of O(n).
A tree keyed by character rather than value. The structure follows the shape of the data, not the data's order.
A tree with a weaker promise — only the top is sorted — and that weaker promise is exactly what makes it fast.
Tree recursion where you build the tree as you walk it. Choose, recurse, un-choose — the template behind every search below.
A tree that is allowed cycles. Same traversals, one new obligation: remember where you have already been.
Backtracking that stops recomputing itself. Write the brute-force recursion first, then memoise it — DP is the second step, never the first.
Commit to the locally best choice and prove you never regret it. Sorting plus a heap is the usual machinery.
Compose the structures instead of using one: an LRU cache is a hash map plus a linked list. Nothing new, everything combined.
The deepest node on the map, and it earns it: Dijkstra is BFS with a heap, and Floyd–Warshall is DP on a graph.
